body_markdown:
First and foremost, Happy Thanksgiving, friends. We’re grateful that you visit our pages, and hope that this week’s festivities treat you well. In addition to sharing time with you, we at Hagerty Media are thankful for a great many things. The folks who surround us; our health; our cars; and, of course, tools. Certain implements our staff couldn’t imagine doing without—check them out below, and let us know what you’d add to the list. Gobble, gobble!


## Flex-Head Ratchet


[Nathan Petroelje](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nathan-petroelje/)


We did a[similar story](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/8-tools-were-thankful-for/) to this a few years back, and in that version, I mentioned how thankful I was for a battery-powered impact gun that saved me loads of time on certain projects.


I’d like to flip it a bit here. Last Christmas, I got a 14-inch flex-head ratchet with a 3/8-inch drive on it. It’s a brute, but also beautiful at the same time. There are plenty of projects where saving time is great, but I’ve come to appreciate the slower, manual nature that using a hand ratchet like this entails. As an added plus, I think it’s forced me to be more deliberate with each step in a project.


I recently replaced the front brakes on my 2016 GMC Sierra, and that ratchet had enough oomph to bust rusty caliper bracket bolts loose. As I was reassembling, the slower pace actually helped my ADHD brain to catch a (nearly) missed step. — *Nathan Petroelje*


## Christmas-Light Stick


Warner Bros.


The tool I am thankful for is not car-related, but I am going to share it anyway. The day after Thanksgiving is when we Eckarts traditionally put up[Christmas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/christmas-carspotting-12-cars-that-featured-in-holiday-classics/) lights. We moved to a new house in a new neighborhood in 1993, and my dad, being the Clark Griswold that he was (still is), couldn’t wait to share his holiday spirit with the new neighbors.


Right after breakfast that Friday morning after Thanksgiving, he enlisted my help in putting up the lights. We got the boxes out and unwound the strands. He’d already screwed the little hooks in under the eaves a week or two before, so all we had to do was hang them. Up the ladder he went, light strand in hand, along with a six-foot piece of 1x trim board with a nail hammered in at an angle on the end.


This was the light-hanging tool. Simple as could be, made from a scrap of wood and a nail to help guide the Christmas-light wire over the hooks in the eaves. It made hanging lights a breeze; he methodically hung the wire onto the end of the stick and reached up to set it in the eaves hooks while I stopped the wire from bouncing into the house or getting caught on the bushes below.


“When you write my eulogy, son, I want you to tell everyone about this stick,” he said from the top of the ladder that day. He was kidding, of course. But we were the only house on the street with Christmas lights that year. The next year there were a few more, and more still the year after that, till practically the whole formerly stodgy neighborhood had lights up. It started with one guy and his very basic invention. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Impact Guns


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I’d typically say it before every Christmas: Just get me tools. Pretty much have three of everything I need now, which is great, because I don’t know where two of them are. As Nate mentioned,[power impact wrenches](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/20-air-and-electric-impact-wrench-myths-tested/) —battery-powered, corded, and even a pneumatic or two—have risen to the top on my must-have list, and the older I get, the more I value them. I would hate to calculate how many lug nuts I have on the property, and I would hate even more having to twist them all off and put them back on by hand with my four-way lug wrench. Coming in a close second would be quality battery chargers, both small (Battery Tenders) and large, most notably an ancient steel Schumacher that is surface-rusting under the paint, but will just *not* give up. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## A Bag


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Is a tool bag a tool? Because the thing that makes my tools both portable and conformable has been a silent hero in my workspace. I recently bought a tool bag as a “go bag” for road trips and[junkyard runs](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-build-the-perfect-junkyard-tool-kit/) , and I’ve realized just how fantastic it is for 90% of what I need. — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Flare-Nut Wrench


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Earlier this year, I had to change the O2 sensors on my wife’s Mustang, only a year after changing the original set that had lasted more than a decade. It had been long enough that I forgot which tools I had used, exactly, but I remembered that I’d purchased a special O2 sensor socket that had helped. The first one came out easily using the socket. “Boy, I sure was smart to get the right tool last time,” I thought to myself, so smitten by the ease with which the first sensor was replaced. The passenger side sensor, jammed in close to the firewall, seemed to sense my self-satisfaction. It silently declared war. If I had been watching, I think I would have seen the whole engine shift, ever so slightly, closer to the firewall to shore up its flanks. After much cursing and repositioning and dropping of said specialty socket, I decided that it just wasn’t going to work. Once I stopped seeing red, I remembered that last time I might have just used a flare-nut wrench. All that to say I’m thankful that I had the right tool all along. Hopefully I won’t get tunnel vision the next time.


Bonus tool: the 36mm socket I needed to remove the axles from my Dana 30 and change the wheel bearings. — *Brandan Gillogly*


## Motorcycle Lift


Kyle Smith


I have a core kit of tools I’m very fond of, but I’m thankful for all of them and the variety of capabilities they enable. However, one I can call out specifically is the simple hydraulic motorcycle lift that has been a staple of my garage floor nearly since day one in this shop.


I had convinced myself I was going to buy a fancier one when I saved up a few more pennies, but a friend’s wife got him one of the budget-conscious models, and I saw the molehill from a fresh perspective. I don’t actually lift bikes up and down on this lift much. I’m not a high-production shop.


So it’s not the actual utility I cherish, but merely the bonus that it is also a wonderful display stand for some of my long-term projects to sit on. Some of those projects end up sitting in one place long enough that even just moving the whole thing up and down is enough of a perspective shift to reinvigorate the drive to pick up tools.


I also can’t afford a lift for my cars, or I would be writing about how thankful I am to have that. — *Kyle Smith*
